headline: Best Personal AI Agents in 2026: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Gemini Spark and More, Compared on Memory, Security and Cost
summary:
A personal AI agent runs continuously, keeps memory across sessions, and acts inside your apps. You talk to it in a chat app, by email or by voice. It keeps working after you close the window.

The category started small. OpenClaw began in November 2025 as Clawdbot, a weekend project by Peter Steinberger. Twelve months later, Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity all ship their own versions.

The products split into 2 camps. Self-hosted agents run on your machine or server and use any model you choose. Managed agents run on a vendor’s cloud VM and come bundled with a subscription.

How we ranked them

We scored each agent on 3 axes that matter once an agent holds your inbox and credentials.

  • Memory: what persists, where it is stored, and whether you can read, edit or delete it.
  • Security: default permissions, the isolation boundary, approval gates, and the public incident record.
  • Cost: the subscription price, or token spend plus hosting for self-hosted options.

Facts come from vendor documentation, launch posts and independent security research. Prices are US list prices as of November 21, 2026. Ranking reflects overall fit for an individual user, not raw capability.

Comparison table

1. Hermes Agent (Nous Research)

What it is: Hermes Agent is an open-source agent from Nous Research.

It runs from a terminal UI, a native desktop app, a local web dashboard and messaging gateways. Parallel counts about 25 supported platforms as of October 2026, including Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Teams and email. Native iMessage arrived in June 2026.

Memory: Memory is the main reason to pick Hermes. It keeps persistent MEMORY.md and USER.md files and curates them with periodic nudges. Session history sits in SQLite with FTS5 full-text search and LLM summarization. Pluggable providers include Honcho user modeling plus 8+ community backends.

Hermes also writes its own skills. It turns completed complex tasks into reusable skills and refines them over time. Skills follow the agentskills.io standard. The /learn command captures a workflow as a slash command without hand-writing SKILL.md.

Security: The docs describe a 7-layer defense-in-depth model. Layers include user allowlists, DM pairing and human approval for destructive commands. Approval mode can be manual, smart (an auxiliary LLM rates risk) or off.

The defaults fail closed. An unanswered approval prompt is denied after 300 seconds. Your own deny rules survive even YOLO mode.

Nous is explicit about the limits. Its docs say the denylist does not sandbox a hostile or compromised agent. The project’s SECURITY.md names OS-level isolation as the one load-bearing boundary. For broad tool access, use a container backend such as Docker, Modal, Daytona or Vercel Sandbox.

Cost: The agent is free. You pay for model tokens from any provider: OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, or local runtimes like Ollama and vLLM. Nous Portal is optional, with Free, $20, $100 and $200 monthly tiers. Local models cut token spend to zero; see the one-click local model setup.

Comments: Hermes is the best open-source pick for most developers. It pairs the deepest memory stack with fail-closed defaults. Setup is still terminal-first, and the local backend offers no protection from a compromised agent.

2. OpenClaw (OpenClaw Foundation)

What it is: OpenClaw defined the category. It started in November 2025 as Clawdbot and went viral in January 2026.

OpenClaw 2.0 shipped as v2026.8.1 on August 31, 2026, built by 933 contributors. The latest release we covered is 2026.9.5, with atomic updates and plugin hot reload.

A central Gateway process routes messages, runs cron jobs and hosts a Control UI. OpenClaw reached 26 channels as of v2026.6, including WhatsApp, Telegram, iMessage, Teams, Matrix and Signal. Supported models include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, xAI, Kimi, Ollama and OpenRouter.

Memory: OpenClaw stores behavior in human-editable Markdown files. SOUL.md holds the persona, TOOLS.md the tool rules and USER.md what the agent knows about you. Version 2.0 moved session and transcript storage into SQLite for better persistence.

This design is transparent. You can open, diff and back up every memory file with ordinary tools.

Security: This is OpenClaw’s weak point. The default mode gives full host access, which WIRED called incredibly risky. An opt-in sandbox runs sessions in per-session Docker containers. It defaults to no network egress, a read-only root and all capabilities dropped.

The incident record is long. CVE-2026-25253 allowed one-click remote code execution via a WebSocket origin bypass. Visiting a malicious page was enough to steal auth tokens. It was patched quickly.

The skills registry was the bigger problem. Koi Security audited 2,857 ClawHub skills and found 341 malicious entries. 335 traced back to one campaign, now tracked as ClawHavoc. Antiy CERT later counted 1,184 malicious skills as the registry grew.

OpenClaw responded. It now scans every uploaded skill with VirusTotal and re-scans daily. Version 2.0 added protected credential requests and a team-scoped Secret Store. Treat ClawHub as untrusted code anyway.

Cost: OpenClaw is free under MIT. A survey of managed hosts found plans from about $12 to roughly $49 per month. Watch the heartbeat check. With expensive models, it can drive significant token spend.

Comments: Pick OpenClaw for channel breadth and the largest ecosystem. Turn on the sandbox, skip unvetted skills, and keep the gateway on loopback. For a deeper head-to-head, see our OpenClaw vs Hermes Agent comparison.

3. Gemini Spark (Google)

What it is: Google unveiled Spark at I/O on May 19, 2026. It runs on Gemini 3.5 Flash with Google’s Antigravity harness. Each user gets dedicated VMs in Google Cloud, so tasks continue with your devices off.

Spark works natively across Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, YouTube and Google Maps. MCP connections extend it to third-party apps. You can message it by text and email, and a macOS app shipped in June.

Memory: Spark’s memory is your Google account. It pulls context from the apps you connect through Personal Intelligence. Google has not documented a separate, editable memory store like Hermes or OpenClaw.

Security: You choose which services Spark can see. Google says it checks in before high-stakes actions such as spending money or sending email. Purchases run through Google’s Agent Payments Protocol, with merchant and transaction limits plus user approval.

Two caveats apply. The product page tells users to supervise closely and interrupt when needed. A leaked early onboarding screen warned that Spark may share your info or make purchases without asking.

There is one structural upside. Spark cannot directly access files on your local system. That limits the blast radius on your own machine.

Cost: Spark launched on the $99.99 AI Ultra plan. Since July 2026 it is included in the $20 US AI Pro plan. The Ultra global rollout excludes the EEA, Switzerland, the UK and Nigeria.

Comments: Spark is the easiest choice if your life already runs on Google Workspace. It is also the cheapest managed agent here. You trade portability: memory and actions stay inside Google’s ecosystem.

4. OpenAI dots (OpenAI)

What it is: OpenAI launched dots at DevDay on September 29, 2026. Each dot runs on GPT-6 Astra with its own cloud computer and browser. Plugins connect it to more than 4,000 apps.

You reach the same dot in ChatGPT, Slack, Microsoft Teams or a voice call. Texting is a limited beta for some US Pro users. For heavy work, a dot hands tasks to ChatGPT Work or Codex. OpenAI says the Codex harness powering dots is open source.

Memory: A dot draws on the conversation, relevant ChatGPT memory and its own saved notes. Those notes cover your preferences, decisions and ongoing work. Switching channels does not start a new dot or reset its memory.

Security: Between requests, a dot runs proactive research across connected apps. That research is read-only; follow-up actions need the right permissions. Your computer stays separate unless you connect it.

For website logins, dots use saved passwords without exposing them to the model. You can open the dot’s computer at any time and press Take over.

Cost: Your first dot is included. Chatting with it does not count toward ChatGPT limits, but its Codex and Work tasks do. Reports differ on the entry plan. BGR says dots require Pro 200 or Business Premium, not the $100 Pro tier. Check OpenAI’s plan page before you buy. The Pro rollout excludes the EEA, Switzerland and the UK.

Comments: Dots suit people who already live in ChatGPT and Codex. Memory carries cleanly across channels, and the read-only research default is sensible. It is the most expensive way into this category.

5. Meta Muse (Meta)

What it is: Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026. It is powered by Meta’s Muse Spark model. You reach it through iOS and Android apps, muse.ai and WhatsApp. A Mac app followed on September 19.

Memory: Muse remembers what matters to you and makes unprompted suggestions. You can tell it to forget specific things it has learned.

Security: Muse has the most detailed published isolation design of the managed agents. It runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated machine that holds both the agent and your data. A separate Sentinel agent sits on the same VM, isolated at the system level.

Muse cannot reach the internet unless Sentinel approves. Sentinel asks you for permission when needed. Muse also asks before sending email or making a purchase, and keeps an audit trail.

Credentials go into secure storage that Muse can use without seeing. Checkout runs through Link by Stripe, which issues one-time-use cards. Meta says it plans a Muse Confidential VM encrypted with a key only you hold.

Cost: Muse has a free tier along with $20 and $100 monthly plans. It launched in the US, then expanded to Singapore and Australia.

Comments: Muse is the best free starting point for errands, shopping and scheduling. Its Sentinel design is a real architectural answer to prompt injection. Until the confidential VM ships, your data still sits on Meta’s cloud.

6. Perplexity Personal Computer (Perplexity)

What it is: Personal Computer merges Perplexity’s cloud agent with your local Mac. It needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later, and Perplexity recommends a Mac mini for 24/7 work. You can start and approve tasks from an iPhone.

The agent works with local files, native Mac apps and the web. Recent updates added hybrid compute that routes sensitive steps to a local model. Multiagent mode runs up to 16 agents that cross-check work.

Memory: Perplexity has not published a detailed memory model for Personal Computer.

Security: On Mac, a privacy gate and local model handle sensitive steps inside an isolated sandbox. Remote tasks on your desktop use 2FA. Perplexity also logs a full audit trail of agent actions.

Cost: Personal Computer requires a Pro or Max subscription. Rework lists Pro at $17/month and Max at $167/month on annual billing. Cloud work consumes credits.

Comments: This is the strongest option for Mac users who want an agent inside local files and apps. It has no chat-app channels, so you control it from Perplexity’s own apps.

7. Hardened OpenClaw alternatives: NanoClaw, IronClaw, ZeroClaw

OpenClaw’s security record spawned a wave of smaller, stricter forks. NeuralTrust’s October 2026 review shortlists Hermes, NanoClaw, ZeroClaw and IronClaw as the main open-source options.

  • NanoClaw runs each agent group in its own Linux container that sees only mounted paths. In March 2026 it partnered with Docker to run agents inside MicroVM sandboxes.
  • IronClaw is a Rust rewrite that runs untrusted tools in a WebAssembly sandbox. Secrets are injected at the host boundary.
  • ZeroClaw is a minimal Rust binary. Composio says it runs on $10 hardware with under 5MB of RAM.

These projects trade ecosystem size for safety. Pick one when you handle regulated data or run tools you did not write. NVIDIA’s OpenShell sandbox work is also worth a look for hardening existing OpenClaw setups.

Also worth watching

  • Claude (Anthropic): Rework lists folder-scoped access and approval before deletions, included in Claude Pro and higher plans.
  • Manus: credit-based billing and an unusual 2026: it joined Meta, then resumed independent operations on September 1.
  • Lindy: Team plan from $29.99/month for 3,000 credits; positioned as a work teammate.
  • Poke: Free, $19 and $199 tiers, reached through Messages, WhatsApp and Telegram.
  • Kimi Work: Moonshot AI’s local desktop agent, reportedly running a 300-subagent swarm.

Memory compared

The agents fall into 3 memory designs:

  • Files you own: Hermes and OpenClaw store memory as Markdown on your disk. You can read, edit, diff and back it up.
  • Vendor notes plus account context: dots and Muse keep their own notes and learned preferences. You can ask them to forget, but you cannot open the store directly.
  • Account as memory: Spark relies on your Google data rather than a separate memory file.

If portability matters, choose files you own. Hermes and OpenClaw memory survives a model switch or a move to new hardware. Back up Hermes’s data directory before migrating machines.

Security compared

The key question is where the isolation boundary sits:

  • Managed agents (Spark, dots, Muse) run on vendor VMs, away from your laptop. Muse adds a second agent that gates network access.
  • Hermes puts approval prompts in front of risky commands and fails closed. Real isolation needs a container backend.
  • OpenClaw gives full host access by default. Its sandbox is strong once enabled, but you must turn it on.
  • Forks like NanoClaw and IronClaw make isolation the default.

Whichever you choose, apply 5 rules:

  1. Run self-hosted agents in a container, VM or dedicated machine.
  2. Grant read-only access first; add send and purchase rights later.
  3. Install skills only from sources you have reviewed.
  4. Keep approval gates on for email, payments and deletions.
  5. Review the audit trail weekly for the first month.

For isolation options, see our ranking of the best agent sandboxes.

Cost compared

Cost works differently across the 2 camps:

  • Self-hosted (Hermes, OpenClaw, forks): the software is free. You pay model tokens plus hosting, or nothing beyond hardware if you run local models.
  • Managed (Spark, dots, Muse, Perplexity): a flat subscription covers compute and the model, subject to usage limits.

Always-on agents burn tokens even when idle. Heartbeat checks, scheduled jobs and proactive research all call the model. On a frontier API, that background load can exceed your chat usage.

To control spend on self-hosted agents, route background work to a cheap or local model. Our ranking of open-source agent harnesses for local LLMs covers that setup.

Which one should you pick?

  • You want your data on your disk and any model: Hermes Agent, on a container backend.
  • You need WhatsApp, iMessage and the most integrations: OpenClaw, with the sandbox enabled.
  • You live in Gmail and Google Docs: Gemini Spark on AI Pro.
  • You already pay for ChatGPT Pro: OpenAI dots.
  • You want a free tier for errands and shopping: Meta Muse.
  • You work on a Mac with local files: Perplexity Personal Computer.
  • You run untrusted tools or regulated data: NanoClaw or IronClaw.

FAQ

  • What is the best personal AI agent in 2026? For developers, Hermes Agent offers the best mix of memory and safe defaults. For non-technical users, Gemini Spark and Meta Muse are the easiest to start with.
  • Is OpenClaw safe to use? It can be, with hardening. Enable the sandbox, keep the gateway on loopback, and avoid unvetted ClawHub skills.
  • Which personal AI agent is free? Hermes Agent, OpenClaw and the hardened forks are free software; you pay for model tokens. Meta Muse has a free tier.
  • Do personal agents run when my computer is off? Managed agents do, because they run on cloud VMs. Self-hosted agents need an always-on machine, such as a home server or Mac mini.

headline: Google AI Previews Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API for Large Tool Libraries
summary:
Google has launched Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API, now in preview in the Interactions API. Gemini API Tool Retrieval lets an agent keep a large tool library available. It does not send every parameter schema in every prompt. The model loads a schema only when a task needs that tool. For agents wired to dozens of functions or MCP servers, it targets a real cost: tool definitions. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

TL;DR

  • Tool: An API feature with no stated tool cap. Google advises static loading under 20 stable tools.
  • Runs on: Google’s servers (server-side search) or your own registry (client-side). Interactions API, v1beta only.
  • Performance: Search, schema load and function call resolve in 1 API request in server mode.
  • Best: 0 extra round trips and no index to host for server-side retrieval.

What is Gemini API Tool Retrieval?

Tool Retrieval is a Gemini API feature that defers tool parameter schemas until the model asks for them. Google’s documentation states the problem plainly. A few dozen function declarations can consume tens of thousands of tokens on every request.

With deferral, the model sees only each tool’s name and a short description. It does not see the parameter schema until retrieval.

How does defer_loading work in the Gemini Interactions API?

You add {"type": "tool_search"} to the tools array. Then you set defer_loading: true on each function to hold back. The @googledevs launch post shows a deferred issue_refund function on gemini-4-hydrogen. Its code comment mentions 50+ other deferred functions.

When the model needs a deferred tool, the response contains 3 steps:

  • tool_search_call: the model requests a tool by name.
  • tool_search_result: the API returns the full schema.
  • function_call: the model emits the call your code executes.

The API resolves the first 2 steps itself. Your app only runs the function_call and returns a function_result.

Deferred functions can carry an optional short_description. It is shown during retrieval and is valid only when defer_loading is true.

Server-side vs client-side retrieval

Server-side is the default. Gemini runs the search, so there is no index to build or host.

Client-side mode uses "execution": "client". Your app runs its own lookup, such as an embedding index, registry or permission filter. It returns matching declarations in function_result.result. Those tools can join mid-conversation, even if absent from the initial tools array. Each client-side search costs 1 extra round trip.

The 2 modes cannot be combined in 1 request. Only 1 tool_search entry is allowed per request.

Does it work with MCP servers and prefix caching?

Yes on both, with caveats. Setting defer_loading: true on an mcp_server entry defers every tool that server exposes. Deferred MCP tools still execute remotely through the Gemini API MCP support.

On caching, deferred schemas stay out of the prompt prefix. Loaded schemas append inline, so implicit caching still applies. The docs add one catch: deferring tools can shrink a prompt below the minimum cacheable size.

What does Tool Retrieval cost?

There is no separate fee. Tokens bill at the model’s standard input, cached and output rates. Each server-side search triggers an extra model call over the full context. Those tokens appear in total_tool_use_tokens, billed at the input rate.

Each loaded schema then stays billed as input for the rest of the conversation. The docs say static loading can cost less for small libraries or per-turn searches.

How does it compare with Claude and OpenAI tool search?

Anthropic and OpenAI already ship similar tool search features, with published savings numbers.

Anthropic and OpenAI figures are self-reported in their own tests. They are not comparable to any Gemini result.

Key Takeaways

  • Gemini API Tool Retrieval defers tool schemas until the model requests them.
  • Server mode resolves search, load and call in 1 API request.
  • Client mode supports custom registries, at 1 extra round trip per search.
  • No extra fee, but loaded schemas stay billed and cannot be unloaded.
  • Google published no savings data; Anthropic reports 85%, OpenAI 47%.

Check out the Google blog post, the Tool Retrieval docs and the MCP function calling docs. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

headline: How AI Models Think, and Where They Run: From One Weight to a GPU Server
summary:
Everyone’s impressed by what AI can do. Here’s how a model actually works, and why running one takes GPUs that cost more than a car.

What Happens When You Send a Prompt

Every time you send a prompt to a language model, whether small, medium or large, you make an API call from a device and get an answer back in seconds. It feels instant, but behind the scenes a lot of work happens to produce that answer.

Every model also has limits it must work within. The most common ones are:

  • Capacity limits: The model can only read and respond within a fixed token limit.
  • Knowledge limits: The model only knows what was in its training data, up to its cutoff date.
  • Behavioral limits: Safety training, usage policies, system prompts and guardrails decide what it will and won’t do.
  • Governance limits: Data privacy and residency rules, regulations, and audit and observability requirements decide how and where it can operate.

Start Simple: A Very Basic Model

Imagine a very small machine. You give it an input, and it always gives you the same output for that input.

This machine takes any number X, adds 5 to it every time, and returns X + 5. Give it 10, and you get 15. Give it 100, and you get 105.

In LLM terms:

  • X is your prompt (the input).
  • 5 is the model parameter: what the machine has “learned.”
  • X + 5 is the model’s response (the output).

Making the Model a Little Smarter

Now let’s make our machine a little smarter. Instead of just adding a number, it multiplies the input by one value and adds another:

Output = (w × X) + b

Here w (weight) and b (bias) aren’t chosen by us. The machine learns them by looking at thousands of examples.

  • Weight (w) controls how much influence the input has on the output.
  • Bias (b) is the model’s built-in starting point before it considers the input.

In fact, our first machine was this same formula with w = 1 and b = 5.

Weight and Bias in the Housing Market

Weight decides how much an input affects the price:

  • Large weight: a small change in the input causes a big change in the output.
  • Near-zero weight: the input hardly matters.
  • Negative weight: the output goes down as the input goes up.

For example, if w = 2,000, every extra square foot adds ₹2,000 to the price. If the model learns a negative weight for “age of house,” older houses get cheaper.

Bias is the starting point: the output you get before any input is counted. It’s a fixed amount added at the end.

For example, if b = ₹1,00,000, the house has a base value of ₹1 lakh before its size is even considered. You can think of it as the value of the land or a market baseline.

So a 1,000 sq ft flat would be priced at:

(2,000 × 1,000) + 1,00,000 = ₹21,00,000 (₹21 lakh)

Putting them together, imagine a line on a graph:

  • The weight sets how steep the line is (the slope).
  • The bias sets where the line starts (the intercept, the point where it crosses the vertical axis).

Training is just the machine trying different slopes and starting points until the line fits the data best.

Our two machines side by side:

  • The +5 machine: w = 1, b = 5. It passes the input through unchanged and adds 5.
  • The house-price machine: w = 2,000, b = ₹1,00,000. It charges ₹2,000 per sq ft, starting from ₹1 lakh.

From Two Parameters to Billions

Our house-price model has just two parameters. A real house price depends on much more: location, floor, number of bedrooms, distance to the metro, the builder’s reputation. Each new factor brings its own weight. Stack thousands of these small machines in layers, with each layer passing its output to the next, and you get a neural network.

An LLM is the same idea at a huge scale. Its input isn’t square footage but your prompt, broken into tokens. Its output isn’t a price but the most likely next word. And its parameters don’t number two. They number in the billions, each one a weight or bias learned from huge amounts of text.

No single weight “knows” anything. Just as no single factor sets the price of a flat in Mumbai, the intelligence comes from billions of them working together.

And all those billions have to live somewhere. A 70-billion-parameter model needs about 140 GB of memory just to hold its weights, before it answers a single question. Every time you make an API call, those weights, already loaded on GPUs, are multiplied against your prompt, and the result is sent back to you as an answer in seconds, for thousands of people at once.

A model’s knowledge lives in its weights. But billions of weights are useless if there’s nowhere fast enough to run them.

So where do those 140 GB (70 billion weights at the standard 2 bytes each) actually live? What does the work when you send a request? And why do the GPUs behind it cost more than a car?

Let’s find out, starting with some basics.

Transformers: How the Model Thinks

Our house-price example needed only a handful of weights. Today’s models can summarize a 100-page document. To make that possible, the weights grow into the billions and the model grows into many layers stacked on top of each other. The output of one layer becomes the input to the next.

This entire network of layers is called a transformer. What makes it special is a mechanism called attention: at every layer, each word looks at the other words in the input to work out which ones matter most for its meaning.

In simple terms, the transformer is the formula (like the house-price calculator from earlier). It’s written once in code and is broadly the same across GPT, Llama and Claude. What makes them different is not the formula; it’s the weights (like the price per square foot).

The formula (the transformer) is only a few pages of code; the knowledge is in the weights. A real model doesn’t have one or two weights; it has billions of them. These billions of weights are what training produces, and together they can take up tens or even hundreds of GB. They are simply files sitting on a disk, and their size varies from model to model. Before the model can answer a single request, all of its weights have to be loaded into memory.

One may ask: why can’t a large model run well on a personal computer or a small server? To understand, let’s look at how a normal laptop or server performs a calculation.

Why a Large Model Doesn’t Fit in a Laptop: CPU and RAM

You open the calculator on your laptop and calculate 100 × 2. What happens? The calculator responds with 200. Behind the scenes, the CPU and RAM are doing all the work.

See the diagram below.

When you ask it to calculate 100 × 2, this is how it works: the computer saves the instructions in RAM, the CPU fetches the instructions from RAM, computes the result, and saves it back to RAM. Here the CPU is doing all the work, while RAM acts as temporary storage, holding the instructions and data the CPU is currently working on.

This setup has three limits when it comes to running a large model:

1. A normal laptop has a limited number of CPU cores. The latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors offer 6, 8, 12 or 16 cores, so a laptop can process only a small number of calculations in parallel, compared with the thousands of cores in a GPU.

2. A typical laptop has 16–32 GB of RAM, whereas a rack server may have 512 GB or more, but the weights of the largest models can go beyond even that.

3. Data moves between the CPU and RAM over a fairly narrow channel: roughly 77–128 GB/s on a laptop, and a few hundred GB/s on a large server. That sounds fast, but a model has to read all of its weights for every word it generates. Even if a 140 GB model fit in a laptop’s memory, at 100 GB/s it would take more than a second per word.

Where the Model Lives and Works: GPU and VRAM

To run a large model quickly, we need three things: thousands of cores working in parallel, hundreds of GB of memory, and a very fast link between the two. Get all three, and the LLM can answer our requests much faster.

That’s exactly what NVIDIA’s GPUs and their VRAM provide, solving each of the problems we discussed earlier.

1. Parallel processing: A basic or entry-level modern NVIDIA GPU typically has around 2,560 to 3,840 CUDA cores (such as the GeForce RTX 5050 with 2,560 CUDA cores and RTX 5060 with 3,840 CUDA cores), while high-end models reach 10,000 to over 21,000. Each CUDA core is far simpler than a CPU core, but together they can do thousands of small calculations at once, which is exactly what a model needs.

2. Memory capacity: A basic or entry-level modern NVIDIA GPU typically comes with 8 GB of VRAM (such as the GeForce RTX 5050 and RTX 5060), while mid-range models offer 12 GB to 16 GB and flagship cards reach 32 GB (RTX 5090). That’s still far short of 140 GB, which is why serious models run on data-center GPUs such as the H100 (80 GB) or B200 (192 GB), often several linked together.

3. Memory bandwidth: Data transfer between a GPU chip and its VRAM typically ranges from 320 GB/s on entry-level cards to 1,792 GB/s on flagship gaming GPUs, and reaches 3,000–8,000 GB/s on data-center GPUs.

Unlike the CPU and RAM, the GPU and its VRAM sit on the same card (on data-center GPUs, the same chip package), connected by a much wider channel. That is what lets data move at such high speed.

The table below compares cores and memory (source: Intel and NVIDIA websites).

Who Drives It: Software and Model Servers

A chip on its own can’t do anything useful; something needs to drive it. That’s where software comes in: CUDA, NVIDIA’s platform for programming its GPUs, and PyTorch, the popular framework built on top of it that most AI models are written in. With a few lines of PyTorch code, you can load a model, ask it a question and get an answer. A very small model can even run this way on your laptop.

In production, though, it’s not just one request: many users can send requests at the same time. So we need something that keeps listening for requests and serves them around the clock. That’s where a model server such as vLLM comes into the picture. vLLM is built on PyTorch; it wraps the model in a service, exposes an HTTP endpoint (an address apps can send requests to), and batches requests from many users together so the GPU stays busy.

A Closer Look at a Model Server

When a model server starts, it loads all the weights into VRAM once. After that, the server stays up and waits for requests.

At its core, the model is a prediction machine: given your input, it predicts the next word. More precisely, it works on tokens, which are words or pieces of words. For each new token, it looks at all the tokens so far (your prompt plus everything it has written) and predicts the next one. It repeats this loop until it predicts a special end token or reaches a length limit. Because the answer is produced one token at a time and sent back as each token is generated, ChatGPT’s reply appears word by word.

A Closer Look at the Token Prediction Loop

When you send a big prompt to ChatGPT, there’s a short delay, and then the answer streams out steadily. The delay is called the prefill step, and the streaming is called the decode (or streaming) step.

The loop has two parts:

1. The prefill step: when you ask a question, your prompt is first converted into tokens. The GPU then processes all of these tokens together, in parallel, in a single pass through the model. Along the way, it saves its intermediate results for each token (called the KV cache) so it never has to redo it. So whether you send 20 tokens or 2,000, the weights are read from VRAM only about once. A longer prompt just means more calculation, which is why a big prompt causes a longer delay. Once the first token is generated, the answer starts appearing on your screen. The time this takes is called TTFT (time to first token).

2. The streaming step: from here, the model produces one token at a time. For every new token, the GPU has to read all of the weights from VRAM again, so this step’s speed is limited by memory bandwidth, not by the number of cores. That’s why the answer streams out at a steady pace, and why fast VRAM matters so much. The delay between two output tokens is called TPOT (time per output token).

TTFT and TPOT are the two basic benchmarks for any LLM serving setup. They depend on the GPU, but also on the model’s size and the model server running it. Prefill speed (TTFT) depends mostly on the GPU’s compute power, while streaming speed (TPOT) depends mostly on its memory bandwidth.

A Closer Look at Caching

The KV cache works well within a single request. However, once the model has responded, the cache is normally cleared, and the model remembers nothing. So the chat app keeps track of the history and sends the entire conversation to the model every time the user asks a question. The model then has to rebuild the KV cache for the whole conversation, again and again. As the chat grows longer, the wait before each answer (TTFT) grows too, and more and more tokens have to be processed.

To solve this, model servers use prefix caching: the server keeps the KV cache for the earlier part of the conversation in VRAM, so when the next message arrives, it only has to process the new tokens. It also saves cost across users: if many requests start with the same text, such as a company’s standard instructions or a shared document, the server works through that shared part once and reuses its KV cache for everyone. The model still writes each answer fresh; it only skips re-reading the part it has already seen.

Wrapping Up

So, where does the model live? In the GPU’s VRAM, where all of its weights are loaded once and stay put. What does the work when you send a request? Thousands of GPU cores, directed by CUDA, PyTorch and a model server such as vLLM. And why do the GPUs cost more than a car? Because a serious model needs tens or hundreds of GB of very fast memory sitting right next to those cores, and often several data-center GPUs linked together.

We also saw how a single request is answered: a prefill step that reads your whole prompt at once (measured by TTFT), then a streaming step that produces the answer one token at a time (measured by TPOT), with caching so the model doesn’t redo work it has already done.

Remember the four limits from the start? Each one now has a physical explanation. The capacity limit exists because every token you send adds to the KV cache in VRAM, and VRAM is finite. The knowledge limit exists because the weights stop changing the day training ends, so the model only knows what it learned. The behavioral limits are partly learned into the weights through safety training and partly layered on top with system prompts and guardrails. And the governance limits decide where those GPUs are allowed to sit and who can see the prompts that pass through them.

So the next time an answer appears in seconds, remember what just happened: your prompt was turned into tokens, run through billions of tiny (w × X) + b calculations on a GPU, and streamed back to you one token at a time. That’s how an AI model thinks, and where it runs.

Coming up next: One GPU, Many Users. So far, we’ve followed a single request. But a real deployment serves thousands of people at once. Next time, we’ll see how one GPU handles many requests at the same time: how the model server batches them together, shares the GPU’s memory between them, and keeps every user’s answer streaming without anyone waiting too long.

headline: A Team of Researchers from Columbia and CertiK Introduce TensorLean for Formal Verification of GPU Kernels
summary:
Researchers from Columbia University and CertiK have introduced TensorLean, a framework for formal verification of GPU kernels at the PTX level. TensorLean is a Lean-based verifier that proves compiled kernels match a tensor-level math spec. The research team checked 149 kernel instances, including every kernel of FlashAttention-2, -3 and -4 plus DeepGEMM. It proved 83 correct. The remaining 66 led to 38 correctness bugs.

TL;DR

  • Size: 1.8K-line PTX parser. Specs total 10,278 lines against 151,285 lines of kernel source, a ratio near 15:1.
  • Runs on: A 16-core workstation. It checks PTX compiled for A100, H100 and B200 kernels.
  • Performance: 83 of 149 kernel instances proved correct, 38 bugs found across 6 projects.
  • Best: Caught a FlashAttention-4 data race that never appeared in 17,760 test runs.

What is TensorLean?

TensorLean is a formal verification framework for GPU kernels at the PTX level.

It starts from unmodified source code. A developer writes a tensor-level spec in Lean. TensorLean then proves 4 properties: no data races, termination, correct output within tolerance, and untouched memory elsewhere.

How does TensorLean verify a GPU kernel?

Specs build on Lean’s Mathlib. Tensor operators follow PyTorch names, so @ means torch.matmul. Each spec has 5 parts: spec_math, spec_mut, spec_layout, spec_tol and requires. The math stays separate from the memory layout.

The pipeline runs in 7 steps:

  1. Start from unmodified source.
  2. Write the tensor-level spec.
  3. Compile to PTX and load a PTX semantics.
  4. Build a happens-before graph to check races and termination.
  5. Symbolically execute to get final memory, identical across schedules.
  6. Lower the spec to PTX-memory level.
  7. Discharge proofs with Lean’s kernel, Z3 and cvc5.

Which techniques make it scale?

  • Concurrency to sequential: Race-freedom proofs on the happens-before graph cover all CTAs, threads and loop iterations symbolically.
  • Loop invariants over semirings: Closed forms for tiled, accumulating loops, such as online softmax, need 1 SMT query per loop.
  • Tolerance proofs: Algebraic error is proved zero. Round-off error is bounded separately, then combined.
  • Assertions as hints: Developers add tensorlean_assert in source. Each is proved once, then reused.

What bugs did TensorLean find?

The GitHub README lists 38 bugs, all reported upstream. FlashAttention accounts for 23. Liger Kernel has 7, TileOPs 3, TileLang 2, DeepGEMM 2 and Triton 1.

By category, the site reports 19 memory access errors and 13 numerical bugs. It also counts 7 data races, 5 uninitialized memory reads and 5 undefined behaviors. There are 3 algorithm errors, 2 miscompilations and 1 deadlock. One bug can sit in several categories.

Of 102 FlashAttention instances, 56 passed all 4 properties. The other 46 each failed a proof goal on a source bug.

&

How does it compare with other GPU kernel verifiers?

The key gap versus Volta is configuration coverage. TensorLean says equivalence checkers unroll loops for one concrete setup at a time. It uses symbolic parameters instead.

Key Takeaways

  • TensorLean proves GPU kernels correct at the PTX level using Lean, Z3 and cvc5.
  • 83 of 149 kernel instances proved correct; 38 bugs found.
  • 23 bugs sit in FlashAttention-2, -3 and -4.
  • Specs run about 15x smaller than the kernel source.

Check out the project page, GitHub repo and announcement on X. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.
